analysis.one_liner: Creates national disclosure rules for rent-to-own contracts and blocks state laws treating them as credit.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 33–21 in 2012 and it sat on the House calendar, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let people take home furniture, appliances, and electronics with weekly or monthly payments and ownership only at the end. This bill would have required stores to tell customers up front the cash price, the full cost to own, and every fee; guaranteed the right to own the item once paid; allowed customers to reinstate after missed payments; and banned harsh contract terms like wage assignments, confessions of judgment, and stacked late fees. At the same time, it would have overridden state laws that treat these deals as credit or require an annualized interest rate to be disclosed, replacing a patchwork of state rules — some stricter, some weaker — with one federal standard that regulates the paperwork but not the price.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-to-own customers — about 2.3 million households a year, mostly lower-income families without credit cards [S4] — would get plain-language disclosure of the total dollars they will pay, a guaranteed path to ownership, the right to reinstate a contract after a missed payment without losing credit for payments already made, and protection from wage assignments, confessions of judgment, unlimited loss-and-damage charges, and multiple late fees on the same missed payment [S4]. Merchants would also benefit, because one federal rulebook would replace state-by-state rules and shield rent-to-own from being regulated as credit anywhere in the country [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Stores must disclose, before signing, the cash price, the payment schedule, and the total cost to acquire ownership, plus every fee separately, on a clearly labeled panel in the contract and on tags at the point of rental [S4].

Customers gain substantive rights: ownership is guaranteed once the disclosed total cost is paid, contracts must be reinstatable after missed payments (60 days after surrender, 120 days if half paid), and agreements cannot contain confessions of judgment, negotiable instruments, wage assignments, security interests in other goods, or more than one late fee per missed payment [S4].
Enforcement includes FTC and state attorney general actions, civil liability for merchants, and criminal penalties for willfully false or missing disclosures [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own merchants bear the cost of new disclosures and liability exposure. Consumers in states with tougher rent-to-own rules would give some of them up: the bill supersedes any state law that regulates these contracts as a credit sale, installment sale, or extension of debt, or that requires disclosure of an annual percentage rate, a time-price differential, or an effective annual rate [S3, S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Merchants; consumers in states with stricter rules

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws requiring an annual percentage rate or time-price differential disclosure, so a customer would see the total dollars owed but never a rate they can compare against a credit card, a layaway plan, or a small loan [S3, S4].
The bill regulates disclosure and contract terms, not price: a rent-to-own contract could still legally cost several times the item's cash price, so long as the total is disclosed [S4].

A company that buys a merchant's contracts can be sued only if the violation is apparent on the face of the agreement, and a customer's signed acknowledgment of receiving disclosures counts as conclusive proof the disclosure was made [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For customers in states with weak or no rent-to-own laws, the bill's real gains — knowing the full cost up front, keeping credit for payments made, and protection from wage assignments and stacked late fees — are meaningful. The price is that it locks in the rent-to-own model as something other than credit: states could no longer require a rate disclosure, which is the one number that makes comparison shopping against other ways to buy possible. Whether that trade favors consumers depends heavily on how protective their state law already was.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved and reported the bill to the House floor calendar in June 2012, but the House adjourned at the end of the 112th Congress without ever taking a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2011 with 14 original cosponsors from both parties and referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S4, S6].
It passed a subcommittee markup in November 2011, then the full committee ordered it reported on May 31, 2012 by a vote of 33 to 21 [S6].
The committee reported the bill with amendments on June 29, 2012 (H. Rept. 112-565) and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 405 [S4, S6].
No floor vote ever followed; the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still on the calendar [S1, S6].
By then the bill had 115 cosponsors, 91 Republicans and 24 Democrats [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own chains in states with strict rules kept operating under the local rules they already had, and no federal preemption arrived; but customers in states with no rent-to-own protections also got nothing, because the bill's disclosure and reinstatement rights never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one: no preemption, no new rights

for.name: 24 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors like Reps. Clay, Meeks, and Towns.

for.name: House Committee on Financial Services
for.what_they_did: Marked the bill up, ordered it reported 33–21, and reported it to the House on June 29, 2012.

against.name: 21 members of the House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee ordered the bill reported by a 33–21 vote on May 31, 2012.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but lopsided: 91 Republican cosponsors to 24 Democratic, and the committee vote of 33–21 shows most of the opposition coming from one side of the aisle.

industries.note: The bill would have locked in the rent-to-own model nationally by keeping it outside credit and usury law and preempting state rules that recharacterize the deals as credit or require a rate disclosure — while also imposing genuine duties on stores, including full cost disclosure, ownership rights, reinstatement rights, and bans on wage assignments and stacked late fees. Customers would see the total dollars owed but never a comparable rate.

industries.industry: Companies that buy or securitize rent-to-own contracts
industries.note: Assignees could be sued only for violations apparent on the face of the agreement, and a customer's signed acknowledgment would count as conclusive proof the disclosures were made, limiting the people these contracts were sold to as an avenue for recovery.

industries.industry: State legislatures and attorneys general setting rent-to-own rules
industries.note: States would lose the power to treat rent-to-own contracts as credit or to require annualized rate disclosures, though state attorneys general would retain authority to enforce the new federal rules in court.
